parts: Every day at midday a 'professional' astrologer spreads out his cowrie shells, a cloth with mystic charts, a notebook and palmyra writing under a tamarind tree in the Town Hall Park. Sacred ash, vermilion, dark whiskers and a saffron turban make his searching eyes look prophetic. He works by the light of the groundnut vendor's flare among sellers of medicine, stolen hardware and cheap cloth.

He knows nothing of the stars. He left his village suddenly, without any plan, and lives on 'study, practice and shrewd guesswork'. He charges three pies a question, lets the client talk for ten minutes, and gives answers about the common troubles of mankind — marriage, money and the tangles of human ties.

One night, as he is packing up, a stranger challenges him. They agree on a wager: eight annas if the answers satisfy, double if they are wrong. By the match-light the astrologer has seen the man's face and is frightened; he tries to give back the anna and leave, but the stranger holds his wrist. The astrologer then tells him that he was stabbed, pushed into a well and left for dead, and even calls him by name — Guru Nayak. He says the attacker died four months ago, crushed under a lorry, and advises Guru Nayak to go home, two days' journey north, and never travel south again.

Guru Nayak gives him a handful of coins — twelve and a half annas, not the promised rupee — and leaves. At home the astrologer tells his wife that a great load has gone from his mind: years ago, as a drunken young gambler, he had stabbed a man in his village and fled believing he had killed him. That man was Guru Nayak, who is alive.

Genre: a suspense story with a surprise ending, first published in 1947; the first story of Malgudi Days. R. K. Narayan received the Sahitya Akademi Award (1960), the Padma Bhushan and the Padma Vibhushan.
Irony: the astrologer calls Guru Nayak a 'swine' who cheated him of a rupee, though he himself has deceived Guru Nayak about who he is and about the 'dead' attacker.
Themes: superstition and gullibility, deception, guilt and redemption, the contrast of light (knowledge) and darkness (secrecy).

Present perfect continuous (has/have been + -ing) for an action continuing up to now; past perfect continuous (had been + -ing) for an action continuing up to a point in the past. Phrasal verbs (put by, put out, look after, look into …).
